title: The Carpenter and the Poem-Lord
markdown:
The moon, a perfect pearl against the velvet of the night sky, cast a gentle glow. It was under such a moon, many seasons ago, that Jun Mori, a carpenter whose skill was as deep and steady as an ancient oak’s roots, worked in his quiet workshop. His hands, rough as bark but gentle as moss, knew the secrets of timber and stone. The scent of sawdust and linseed oil was his perfume, a familiar comfort in the hush of the night. He was known throughout the province for his sturdy, dependable work, the kind that could weather a hundred storms and still stand tall, its joints singing a silent song of resilience. Some stories are carried on the wind, and this is one of them, a tale about craft, and about a lord who perhaps loved poems more than principles.

The lord of the grandest castle in the valley was named Lord Hidetaka. He was a man whose mind was a garden of verses, and whose greatest joy was crafting haiku. A perfect seventeen syllables, he’d often declare, could capture the very essence of a bird’s song or the dewdrop on a spider’s silken thread. He would spend hours meticulously arranging pebbles in his garden, not for their color or texture, but for the stillness they evoked, the silence that hinted at a deeper meaning. Yet, when it came to his castle, his love for poetic perfection sometimes made him a peculiar master. He valued a sweeping eave that mimicked the arc of a heron’s wing more than the sturdy support it needed. The wind often whispered through the eaves of his castle, not just with the rustling of leaves, but with a soft, knowing sigh, as if the very structure was in agreement with the wind's gentle teasing, a silent commentary on the lord's airy notions. Even the squirrels sometimes paused their scurry to cock their heads, as if listening for a hidden stanza.

One crisp autumn morning, the air smelling of fallen leaves and distant woodsmoke, Lord Hidetaka summoned Mori-san. The servants scurried, ensuring the path to the lord’s audience chamber was free of any stray twigs or fallen blossoms that might mar the lord's aesthetic sensibilities. "Mori-san, my dear fellow of timber and truth," he began, his voice as light as a falling petal, his thin mustache twitching with polite anticipation, "I require a new wing for my castle. A wing that speaks of solitude, like a single crane in winter snow, a space that breathes with the quietude of a forgotten shrine."

Mori-san bowed, his eyes, kind and weathered like old oak, scanning the lord’s expectant face. He had seen many lords, many eccentricities, but Lord Hidetaka’s devotion to the abstract was truly remarkable. "Of course, my lord," he replied, his voice a low, steady hum, like the gentle thrum of wood being planed. "And what dimensions shall this wing possess? What manner of supports will be most pleasing to its solitary spirit?"

Lord Hidetaka waved a dismissive hand, a gesture that seemed to scatter the very practicality Mori-san embodied. "Dimensions are for builders of mundane bridges, Mori-san. This wing must be as the echo of a lonely flute. It must feel as if it simply *is*, without the burden of earthly beams. Imagine, if you will, a roof that floats like a cloud, held aloft by the very essence of longing. The pillars, mind you, must be so slender they are mere suggestions, like the memory of bamboo. They must whisper, not shout, their support." He then plucked a fallen maple leaf from his sleeve and held it aloft. "This, Mori-san, is the spirit I seek – ephemeral, yet profound."

Mori-san’s brow furrowed. He looked at the leaf, delicate and dry, and then at the solid, dependable stone of the castle walls. "My lord," he began, choosing his words with the care he would use to fit a joint, "a roof, even one as graceful as a cloud, needs something substantial to hold it against the sky's embrace. A strong wind, you see, can be a boisterous guest, and even the most profound longing requires a solid footing." He pictured the leaf, so easily torn by a gust, and a shiver, not of cold, traced his spine.

Lord Hidetaka chuckled, a sound like dry reeds rustling in a breeze. "Ah, Mori-san, you speak of the practical. But this is not mere construction; this is architectural poetry! I want the feeling of open space, the quiet of the void. Can you not make it so?" He then recited, his voice gaining a reedy enthusiasm, " 'Empty space holds all, / Echo answers silent call, / Nature’s breath is free.' See, Mori-san? The void is key!"

And so it went, a dance between the tangible and the ethereal. Mori-san would sketch designs, carefully showing where strong timbers would hide beneath decorative panels, where deep foundations would anchor the structure against the whims of weather and time. He would explain, with the patience of a river carving its course, how the weight of the roof tiles needed to be distributed, how the walls would need to withstand the pressure of the earth should it decide to shift. But Lord Hidetaka would invariably reject them with a sigh that seemed to carry the weight of unfulfilled poetic dreams. "Too solid, Mori-san! It feels… grounded. I want it to feel as if it could lift off with the morning mist! The pillars must be like ink strokes on rice paper, so fine that the light itself passes through them." He would then recite a haiku about a solitary pine on a windswept cliff, expecting Mori-san to translate that sentiment into wood and plaster, a translation that, to Mori-san's practical mind, seemed akin to asking a squirrel to compose a symphony.

One day, as Mori-san was patiently explaining the necessity of a sturdy crossbeam to support the weight of a particular style of roof tile, Lord Hidetaka sighed dramatically, his thin mustache drooping. "Mori-san, your mind is like a well-worn tool – practical, yes, but lacking imagination. This crossbeam, it is a clumsy word in my poem of a building. It shouts when it should whisper. I want the feeling of open space, the quiet of the void. Can you not make it so?" He gestured vaguely towards the ceiling, which Mori-san had designed with a subtle, supportive curve. "That curve," he declared, "should be a sigh, not a structural necessity."

Mori-san looked at the half-finished wall, its timbers meticulously joined, then up at the darkening sky. The wind, which had been a gentle companion, a soft murmur in the pine trees surrounding the castle, was beginning to tug at the eaves of the existing structure. It carried the scent of rain, heavy and insistent, a scent that always made Mori-san’s bones ache with a familiar premonition. "My lord," he said softly, his voice calm but with an undercurrent of concern, "even the void needs edges to define it. And the wind, it does not care for poetry when it blows with anger. It is a force of nature, not a muse." He paused, as if listening to the wind’s rising chorus. "A castle, my lord, must first be a home. And a home must be safe."

Then, it happened. The sky, which had been a placid blue, turned the bruised color of plums, a dramatic shift that even Lord Hidetaka, lost in his world of verse, could not ignore. The wind, no longer a whisper, began to howl, a lonely lament that grew into a furious shriek, whipping the trees into a frenzy. Rain lashed against the castle walls like a thousand tiny hammers, each drop a percussive beat against the fragile edifice of Lord Hidetaka's poetic vision. The world outside seemed to hold its breath, then release it in a torrent.

Inside the hastily constructed new wing, Lord Hidetaka’s poetic design began to groan. The "whispering pillars," as he had so fondly named them, swayed precariously, their slender forms protesting the unseen forces that sought to bend them into oblivion. A section of the "cloud-like" roof sagged with an alarming groan, and a cascade of water, not like gentle dew but like a playful waterfall, began to pour in, drenching the lord's meticulously arranged calligraphy scrolls. Lord Hidetaka, his face as pale as a moth’s wing, his silk robes suddenly damp and clinging, stared in horror. His beautiful, poetic vision was not just flawed; it was collapsing.

"The ink strokes! They are breaking!" he cried, his voice barely audible above the storm’s deafening roar. He clutched his chest, as if his own heart were being battered by the wind. "My solitude! My empty space!"

Mori-san, without a word, had already grabbed his tools. His movements were not frantic, but purposeful, honed by years of responding to the earth's rumblings and the sky's tempests. He worked with a furious but controlled energy, his understanding of the wood’s language urgent now, as if he were speaking to each piece of timber, coaxing it to hold firm. He hammered in bracing timbers, reinforcing the weak points with a speed and certainty that came from a lifetime of experience. He ignored the decorative flourishes Lord Hidetaka had insisted upon, the delicate carvings of cranes and bamboos that were now a liability, focusing only on making the structure sound. He drove in support beams, not like ink strokes, but like strong, honest arms holding back the deluge, his hammer blows a steady, reassuring rhythm against the storm’s chaos. He even managed a wry, silent thought: "Perhaps these beams can be the roots of my cloud, my lord."

As the worst of the storm passed, leaving behind a sodden, dripping world, the new wing, though scarred and far from the ethereal vision, still stood. It was not a poem; it was a shelter. The "whispering pillars" were now braced by sturdy timbers, their whispers replaced by a quiet resilience. The "cloud-like" roof had a few noticeable dips, a testament to the storm's fury, but it had not surrendered. Lord Hidetaka, shivering but safe, his once-pristine robes splattered with mud, looked at the sturdy, if unpoetic, repairs. He saw the raw strength of the wood Mori-san had used, the clever joinery that had held firm against the storm's onslaught. He noticed how the added beams, though rougher than he’d intended, created a pleasing, almost rugged, pattern that spoke of endurance.

"Mori-san," he whispered, his voice now stripped of its poetic flourish, hoarse with emotion and the residue of fear, "you have saved my castle. You have saved… me." He looked at his hands, which had only ever written verses and arranged flowers, then at Mori-san’s, calloused and strong, their very touch capable of creating such unyielding defense. "I see now. There is a poetry in strength, isn't there? A different kind, perhaps, but just as true. A language spoken not in syllables, but in steadfastness. A haiku of beams and joints."

Mori-san simply nodded, a small, knowing smile gracing his lips. He began to tidy his tools, the scent of wet wood and fresh rain filling the air, a symphony of its own. The storm had passed, and with it, a lesson learned.

In the seasons that followed, Lord Hidetaka did not abandon his haiku. Indeed, he found a new depth in them, a greater appreciation for the strength that allowed for such delicate beauty. But when he commissioned new additions, he would often stand with Mori-san, listening intently as the carpenter explained the whispers of the wood, the strengths of the stone, the hidden harmonies of structural integrity. He learned that beauty could indeed take flight, but it needed good earth beneath it to soar. He discovered that even an empty space could feel profound when it was safely enclosed, that a solitary crane was more poignant when it had a sturdy branch upon which to rest. The trees remember this story well – the tale of the haiku lord who finally understood that even the most elegant poem needs a sturdy frame to truly last, and that sometimes, the simplest truth is the most beautiful of all. And Mori-san? He continued his work, his hands speaking the language of wood and stone, finding quiet satisfaction in building things that would endure, a silent poet of the practical world.
characters: Jun Mori the castle carpenter, Lord Hidetaka the haiku tyrant
